1.pericope_label: Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed, lest we let them slip

schools.summary: Begin with the connecting particle, which is one of cause and is frequent in this Epistle: because Jesus is superior to prophets and angels, and the new revelation superior to the old, the exhortation follows. Note that the writer often pauses in the argument, as here, to drive home a pungent exhortation, and that the verb rendered ought expresses necessity rather than mere obligation. Render the object of the heed simply as the things heard, since this completes the thought of the opening verse, where speaking and hearing both carry weighty emphasis. Then correct the familiar rendering of the last clause. The version that speaks of letting them slip was first introduced by the Genevan Bible; it substantially gives the sense but inverts the figure presented in the Greek, and the words must be rendered lest possibly we drift away, as an older English version had it. The verb is an old one meaning to flow past or glide by, used elsewhere of a river flowing past, and it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. The picture is not of a leaking vessel but of a man being carried along by the current, swept past the sure anchorage which is still within reach; unless the mind be held closely to the words God has spoken, it must drift away from them and from the salvation they promise. On the second verse, render it the word spoken through angels: the word was God's, but they were the medium. Take it of the commands of the Mosaic law, and join the verse to those passages which bring the ministration of angels at Sinai into relief. Admit that the Old Testament yields only one text in illustration, the coming from Sinai amid myriads of holy ones, to which the Greek version adds angels at his right hand, and that two of the Targums speak similarly; then show from Philo and from a speech of Herod recorded by Josephus that such a ministration was a tenet of Jewish belief in the apostolic age. Gloss steadfast as firm and settled, not vacillating: the law determined what crime was and was firm in its punishment, making no provision for indulgence in sin. Distinguish the two nouns for the offence, since they are more than a mere pairing, the one meaning a stepping aside and the other a neglect to hear. On the third verse, ask the question rhetorically and answer it from the greatness of the salvation and the dignity of him through whom it came; and be candid about the verse's admission concerning its author, that he ranks himself with those to whom the word was made sure by them that heard, which stands in striking contrast with the apostle who repeatedly claimed to have received his doctrine directly from the Lord. On the fourth verse, take the compound verb strictly as bearing witness with the preachers, and distinguish the three terms for the miracles: a wonder attracts attention, a power shows whose power is at work, a sign reveals the purpose of God in it.

State the proportion first, for it governs the whole exhortation: the higher the dignity of Christ is than that of angels, the more reverence is due to the Gospel than to the Law. Then meet the objection that must arise, since both Law and Gospel are from God, and to lower the one seems to degrade the majesty of God himself. Answer that he ought indeed always to be heard with equal attention whenever he may speak, and yet that the fuller he reveals himself to us, the more our reverence and attention to obedience should increase in proportion to the extent of his revelation; not that God is in himself less at one time than at another, but that his greatness is not at all times equally made known to us. Then take up the second question, whether the Law also was not given by Christ, which would seem to undo the argument. Reply that the comparison is between a veiled revelation on the one side and a manifest one on the other: in bringing the Law, Christ showed himself but obscurely and as under coverings, so that it is nothing strange the Law should be said to have been brought by angels without any mention of his name, whereas in the promulgation of the Gospel his glory was so conspicuous that he may justly be deemed its author. On the closing clause of the first verse, gather the true sense from the contrast, for to give heed and to let slip are opposites: the first means to hold a thing fast, the other to let it off like a sieve or a perforated vessel, whatever may be poured into it. On the second verse, take firmness to mean authority, since God required the word to be believed, and read the clause about punishment as explanatory of that authority, for it is evident that a doctrine of which God shows himself the avenger is by no means unprofitable or unimportant. On the third verse, press that not only the rejection of the Gospel but also its neglect deserves the heaviest punishment, and that on account of the greatness of the grace which it offers: the more precious the gifts, the baser is our ingratitude when we do not value them. Note that the verb is literally not to care for, and that salvation is here transferred to the doctrine of salvation, since the Lord would have men saved no otherwise than by the Gospel; so that whoever seeks salvation in any other way seeks to attain it by another power than that of God, which is an evidence of extreme madness. On the fourth verse, distinguish the three names given to the miracles and then state their right use, that they serve to establish the Gospel, since almost all the miracles done in all ages were performed to be the seals of God's word.

Give the reason for the exhortation in one sentence: because God has spoken to us by his Son, because that Son is so great and glorious a person, and because the subject addressed to us is of infinite importance to our welfare. Then say what the hearing must be, that we should hear the doctrine of Christ with care, with candour, and with deep concern. On the closing clause, keep the figure of the leaking vessel: the words mean lest at any time we should leak out, which is a metaphor taken from unstanched vessels, whose staves not being close together allow the fluid put into them to escape through the chinks. Superficial hearers lose the benefit of the word preached as an unseasoned vessel loses its liquid; and no one can hear to the saving of his soul unless he give the most earnest heed, which he will not do unless he considers the dignity of the speaker, the importance of the subject, and the absolute necessity of the salvation of his soul. Note that a Greek father read the word differently, as meaning lest we perish or fall away. On the second verse, be careful what is claimed. The word spoken by angels may mean the law delivered by their mediation, as some hold; but the writer probably means those particular messages which God sent by angels, as in the case of Lot. Say plainly that in giving the law God spoke by angels, but in proclaiming the gospel by his Son, and distinguish the two terms for the offence as the commission of sin and the omission of duty, both of which that word punished. On the third verse, define the salvation before pressing the neglect: it is a deliverance from so great wickedness and misery into so great holiness and happiness, first spoken of by him who is Lord of angels as well as men, and confirmed by those who had heard him and were themselves eyewitnesses and ministers of the word. Then set the two dispensations side by side, that the greatness may be felt: the one was for the Jews alone, the other for all mankind; the one was full of types and ceremonies, the other their substance; the one dealt chiefly with the body and outward state, the other with the heart and conscience; the one promised temporal happiness, the other spiritual; the one belonged chiefly to time, the other to eternity. Then define the neglect exactly, for the whole warning turns on it. Those who neglect are not only they who oppose or persecute it, but they who pay no regard to it, who do not meddle with it, do not concern themselves about it, do not lay it to heart, and consequently do not get their hearts changed by it. These cannot escape, not merely because they oppose God's commandment, but because they sin against the very cause and means of their deliverance; and since there is but one remedy by which their diseased souls can be saved, by refusing to apply that one remedy they must necessarily perish.

Proceed in the plain and profitable method of doctrine, reason and use, and mark that this chapter is the application of the truths already proved: having shown Christ to be superior to the angels by whose ministry the law was given, and therefore the gospel dispensation to be more excellent than the legal, the apostle now applies the doctrine both by exhortation and by argument. Take the exhortation first. It is the great concern of every one under the gospel to give the most earnest heed to all gospel discoveries and directions: to prize them highly in his judgment as matters of the greatest importance, to hearken to them diligently in all the opportunities he has, to read them frequently, to meditate on them closely, and to mix faith with them; we must embrace them in our hearts and affections, retain them in our memories, and regulate our words and actions according to them. Then take the motives that enforce it, and let the first be the loss we sustain by neglect. When we have received gospel truths into our minds we are in danger of letting them slip, for our minds and memories are like a leaky vessel, which does not without much care retain what is poured into it; and this proceeds from the corruption of our natures, from the enmity and subtlety of Satan, who steals away the word, and from the entanglements of the world, the thorns that choke the good seed. Say what such a loss amounts to: those who let slip the gospel truths they had received have lost a treasure far better than thousands of gold and silver; the seed is lost, the time and pains in hearing are lost, and the hope of a good harvest is lost, for all is lost if the gospel be lost. Draw the practical rule from it and press it home: this consideration should be a strong motive both to our attention to the gospel and to our retention of it, for indeed if we do not well attend we shall not long retain the word of God, and inattentive hearers will soon be forgetful hearers. Then let the second motive be the dreadful punishment we shall incur, and let it be measured by the argument of the passage, from the lesser to the greater: if the word spoken by angels was so steadfast that every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense, the neglect of a salvation spoken by the Lord himself cannot be a small thing.

debates.question: What is the figure in the words rendered let them slip?

sides.position: Drifting away: the verb means to flow past or glide by, and the picture is of a man carried off by the current, swept past a sure anchorage still within reach
Leaking out: a metaphor from unstanched vessels whose staves are not close, so that what is poured in escapes through the chinks
A Greek father read it differently again, as meaning lest we perish or fall away

debates.question: What is the word spoken by angels?

sides.position: The commands of the Mosaic law, the word being God's while the angels were the medium through which it was given
Not the Law at all, but those particular messages which God sent by angels, as in the case of Lot

debates.question: If both Law and Gospel are from God, how can one claim more reverence?

sides.position: God ought always to be heard with equal attention, but the fuller he reveals himself the more our reverence should rise; and in bringing the Law Christ showed himself only darkly and as under coverings
Because of the supreme dignity of him in whom at the last God speaks, men are bound to give the more earnest heed

outliers.note: Alone refers the word spoken by angels not to the Law but to the particular messages God sent by angels, as in the case of Lot, and alone records that a Greek father read the closing verb as meaning to perish or fall away.

Alone raises and answers the objection that the Law also was given by Christ, replying that in bringing it he showed himself only obscurely and as under coverings, so that it could be ascribed to angels without mention of his name.

themes: we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard
if the word spoken by angels was stedfast
how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation

5.pericope_label: Not unto angels hath he put in subjection the world to come; what is man?

schools.summary: Show the connection both ways before expounding: back to the angels described as ministering spirits sent forth to serve those who shall inherit salvation, and forward to the salvation just spoken of, since the word salvation is what binds this section to the last. Render the verb did he subject rather than hath he put in subjection, for the reference is to the passage quoted in the following verses, which is already in the writer's thought, and the subject is God speaking in the prophetic Scripture. On the phrase the world to come, be exact about the vocabulary: the word here means the inhabited earth, the world of man, and is an entirely different word from the one so translated in a later chapter, which properly relates to time. Ask whether the period is still future or is viewed from the Old Testament standpoint, and answer from the verses that follow, especially the ninth, that the period referred to is the one which succeeds the exaltation of Christ; we ourselves cannot but markedly distinguish the present stage of the kingdom from the future, but in the perspective of prophecy the two were blended. On the citation, note the studious indefiniteness of but one somewhere, which is perfectly indefinite and is a mannerism common in Philo, sometimes used by him where he cannot possibly have been in doubt about his source. Explain why it is used here: as a rule the words of Scripture are quoted in this Epistle as God's own utterances, and since this passage is an address to God that was impossible, so the writer seems glad to avoid mentioning the human prophet. Render testified as solemnly declared, for the words are no light exclamation of wonder. In the question itself, mark that the interrogative is neuter and not masculine, so that the insignificance of man is implied, and that son of man here is not the phrase our Lord used of himself but the literal expression familiar from Ezekiel, without Messianic meaning. Gloss the verb visited as to look upon or look after, the root from which the word for overseer comes. Then state the one point at which the Greek departs from the Hebrew: where the Greek has a little lower than the angels, the Hebrew has a little less than God, a change probably introduced by the translators from the wish, often traceable in their work, to tone down expressions about the Deity which seemed bold. Note also the doubt whether the last clause of the seventh verse belongs to the quotation at all, since it is absent from some very good authorities. On the eighth verse, keep the studious repetition of the leading word audible in translation, and take the argument as it stands: in subjecting all things God left nothing unsubjected, but now we see not yet all things subjected to him. Man's sovereignty was meant to be all-inclusive, and he is crowned king of nature, invested with a divine authority over creation; yet how far short of this destiny has man come, for not even today, with all his triumphs over nature by telescope and microscope, airplane and submarine, steam and electricity and radio, has he reached that goal.

Take the verse as a further proof that Christ ought to be obeyed, since the Father has conferred on him the sovereignty of the whole world while the angels are wholly destitute of such an honour; it follows that none of the angels should stand in the way of his pre-eminence who alone possesses supremacy. Then examine the psalm quoted, for it seems at first unfitly applied to Christ. David there mentions the benefits God bestows on mankind: having contemplated God's power as manifested in the heaven and the stars, he comes to man, in whom the wonderful goodness of God appears in a peculiar manner; he does not, then, speak of any particular person, but of all mankind. Answer that this affords no reason why the words should not be applied to the person of Christ. Grant that man was at first put in possession of the world, that he might rule over all the works of God, but say that by his own defection he deserved the loss of his dominion; it was a just punishment for ingratitude that the Lord, whom he refused to acknowledge and faithfully to worship, should have deprived him of a right previously granted. As soon as Adam alienated himself from God through sin, he was justly deprived of the good things he had received; not that he was denied the use of them, but that he would have had no right to them after forsaking God. Point to the tokens of that loss which God left in the very use of things: the wild beasts ferociously attack us, those who ought to be awed by our presence are dreaded by us, some never obey us and others can hardly be trained to submit, the earth answers not our expectations in cultivating it, and the sky, the air and the sea are often adverse to us. Add that even were all creatures to continue in subjection, whatever the sons of Adam possessed would be deemed a robbery, for what can they call their own when they themselves are not God's? On that foundation the conclusion is evident, that God's bounty belongs not to us until the right lost in Adam is restored by Christ. On the word rendered a little, hold that it means little in degree and not little in time, since that is plainly the meaning in the psalm and there is no reason for a different one here. Admit frankly that the Apostle does not design an exact explanation of the words: there is nothing improperly done when verbal allusions are made to embellish a subject in hand, and he bids us consider the abasement of Christ, which appeared for a short time, and then the glory with which he is perpetually crowned, doing this more by alluding to expressions than by explaining what David understood. On the last clause, meet the objection that all things are not yet subject to Christ either. The answer is that Christ has universal dominion, that the objection is anticipated and admitted, and that what is as yet wanting will in its time be completed.

Read the verse as a proof of what went before, and say why: the greater the salvation is, and the more glorious the Lord whom we despise, the greater will be our punishment. Then define the phrase the world to come from the usage of those to whom the letter was written. Among the Jews it meant the days of the Messiah, and this has often been shown; the administration of that kingdom has not been entrusted to angels, who were frequently employed under the law, for the government is on the shoulder of Jesus Christ, who alone has the keys of death and hell, who alone opens and shuts, and who is Governor of the universe and Head of the Church. Note that others take the world to come for the future glory, referring the words to the angel of God's presence who brought Israel into the promised land, and that a respected commentator contends for this; but the former sense is more consistent with the Jewish phraseology. Add that the dispensation was styled the world to come although it is still in great measure to come, and that in this last great dispensation the Son alone presides. On the citation, explain why it is introduced so indefinitely: it was common thus to express the testimony of any of the inspired writers, and the same form occurs in Philo, and even among the heathen, as when Plato cites a certain person meaning Heraclitus. It is such a mode of quotation as we use when we speak of that great philosopher or that celebrated divine; the mode therefore implies not ignorance but reverence. Then go behind the Greek to the Hebrew, where the variation of terms is very emphatic. The name given to man at his creation expresses his origin and his distinction from other animals; the other word, which signifies sick, weak and wretched, was never given to him until after his fall. That God should remember in the way of mercy these wretched beings is great condescension; that he should visit them, manifest himself to them, dwell among them, and at last assume their nature and give up his life to ransom them, is mercy and love indescribable. Note too that the sense rises: we are mindful of one who is absent, but to visit denotes the care of a present God. On the psalm's occasion, observe that it seems to have been composed on a clear moonlit and starlit night while its author contemplated the fabric of heaven, since in his magnificent description of the luminaries he takes no notice of the sun, the most glorious of them all. And on the words about dominion, allow that they were doubtless in some sense applicable to the first Adam, though in their complete and highest sense they belong to none but the second.

Return here to the pleasant subject of the personal excellency of Christ above the angels, and pursue it further. Lay down the proposition, which is negative in form and positive in substance: the state of the gospel church, here called the world to come, is not subjected to the angels but is under the special care and direction of the Redeemer himself. Neither the state in which the church is at present, nor that more completely restored state at which it shall arrive when the prince of this world is cast out and the kingdoms of the earth shall become the kingdom of Christ, is left to the government of angels; but Jesus Christ will take to him his great power and will reign. Observe the difference between the two dispensations at this very point: he does not make that use of the ministration of angels to give the gospel which he made to give the law, which was the state of the old and now antiquated world. This new world is committed to Christ and put in absolute subjection to him alone in all spiritual and eternal concerns, and he has the administration of the gospel church, which at once bespeaks Christ's honour and the church's happiness and safety. Then state it in the strongest form the passage will bear, and let the reason be felt: it is certain that neither the first creation of the gospel church, nor its after-edification or administration, nor its final judgment and perfection, is committed to the angels, but to Christ; God would not put so great a trust in his holy ones, for his angels were too weak for such a charge. Then turn to the Scripture account of the blessed Jesus to whom the gospel world is put in subjection, and take the words of the psalm in both their senses. As applicable to mankind in general they are an affectionate and thankful expostulation with the great God concerning his wonderful condescension and kindness to the sons of men, in remembering them and in visiting them; as applied here to the Lord Jesus they set out the dignity to which our nature has been raised in him.

Break off the exposition here and speak to the hearers directly, for the doctrine is of no use to a congregation that is not listening. Say plainly that you could have wished to know for certain whether any hear with fitting earnestness the things that are said, or whether the seeds are being cast by the wayside; for in the former case the instruction could be given with more cheerfulness. Then state why you will speak in either case: we shall speak though no one hear, because of the fear laid upon us by our Saviour, who told the prophet to testify to the people and said that even if they hear not, he should himself be guiltless. Yet do not pretend the duty is a pleasure when it bears no fruit. Even if no man hears, and even if the labour, so long as one's own part is fulfilled, brings no danger to the speaker, the labour is not altogether pleasant; for what profit is it, when though the preacher is not blamed, no one is benefited? If the hearers would give heed, we should receive advantage, and that not so much from avoiding punishment ourselves as from their progress. Then propose a method for finding out, and let it be a searching one. Take notice of some who are not very attentive, and question them privately when you meet them; if they are found to retain any of the things that have been spoken, not all, for that would not be very easy, but even a few things out of many, there need be no further doubt about the rest. Admit what would have been fairer still, that we ought, without giving notice beforehand, to have attacked the hearers when they were off their guard; and let the warning stand, that even after notice has been given, the questioning may come when they are not expecting it.

debates.question: What is the world to come?

sides.position: The days of the Messiah, the gospel dispensation, so styled by the Jews though it is still in great measure to come
The inhabited earth, the world of man; the word differs from the one so translated later, and the period meant is the one succeeding the exaltation
Some take it for the future glory, referring the words to the angel of God's presence who brought Israel into the promised land — reported, but less consistent with Jewish phraseology

debates.question: Why is the citation introduced so indefinitely?

sides.position: A studious indefiniteness common in Philo; and since this passage is an address to God it could not be quoted as God's own utterance, so the writer seems glad to avoid naming the prophet
It was a common form of citing an inspired writer, used by Philo and even by Plato of Heraclitus; the mode implies not ignorance but reverence
The writer knew perfectly well, but wrote to Jews conversant with the Scriptures, whose own way of citing was exactly this

debates.question: A little lower than God, or than the angels?

sides.position: The Hebrew has a little less than God, and the change was probably made by the translators from a wish to tone down bold expressions about the Deity
Rightly rendered angels by the Apostle, and so the Targum and the Jewish commentators take it
The Hebrew word is applied to judges elsewhere and is certainly not God in our sense

debates.question: How can a psalm about mankind be applied to one man?

sides.position: Man was put in possession of the world and by his defection lost the right to it, so that God's bounty is not ours until that right is restored in Christ
The dominion given at the creation is broken and is complete only in the second man
Man is crowned king of nature and invested with authority over creation, yet has come far short of that destiny

outliers.note: Alone breaks off exposition to interrogate the congregation, wishing he could know whether any hear with fitting earnestness, and proposing to question the inattentive privately to find how much they retain.

Alone reconstructs the occasion of the psalm, supposing it composed on a clear moonlit and starlit night, since in so magnificent a description of the luminaries the sun, the most glorious of them, is never mentioned.

themes: unto the angels hath he not put in subjection the world to come, whereof we speak
What is man, that thou art mindful of him?
now we see not yet all things put under him

9.pericope_label: But we see Jesus crowned with glory and honour, that he should taste death for every man

schools.summary: Reorder the clauses so the argument is visible: we see him who has been made a little lower than angels, Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honour. Say what that sight answers to. We do not see man triumphant, but we do see Jesus; death has defeated man, and this man has conquered death, and in him alone the divine purpose is fulfilled in all its parts. Note the peculiar fitness of the human name here, for him in whom the Psalmist's words concerning man are literally fulfilled. Then face the apparent departure from the psalm, since the words which there denote dignity here denote humiliation; the difference is not essential, for in each case it is the position of man that is signified, and our Lord's assumption of human nature must in any case be spoken of as a descent to a lower sphere. On the disputed phrase, prefer a little in degree; the rendering a little while is much less probable, though the same words are used of time elsewhere in Scripture. Take the preposition in its causal sense: it is because of the suffering of death that we see him crowned, so that the crowning is not the purpose of the humiliation but the reward of the obedience. Mark also what the verse does not say. We do not read that we see all things put in subjection to him, which would conflict with what is taught later; other words of the psalm are substituted, which do not imply that the complete actual subjection is already accomplished, and the exaltation of the One is not a substitute for the exaltation of the many but is what renders it possible. Then handle the difficulty in the position of the last clause, for it can hardly be said that Jesus was crowned with glory in order that he might taste death. Nearly all the difficulty is removed by remembering that it is on the triumphant issue of the sufferings that their efficacy depends, and that a Christian cannot separate the two even in thought, since in one Gospel we are taught that in his crucifixion Jesus is exalted. On the last phrase, note that to taste death is a familiar Hebraism; the expression occurs in the Gospels but not in the older Greek, and it means to see death, a bitter experience and not a rapid sip. Say plainly that the death was in behalf of every one and not of everything, as some early Greek theologians took it, and record the rival reading which puts apart from God in place of by the grace of God, found in some manuscripts, whatever its origin.

Settle the ambiguity of the words rendered a little before anything else, for the phrase is capable of meaning little in degree or little in time. In the psalm the former is evidently the meaning, and there is no reason for a different meaning here: Christ, in becoming man, assumed a nature inferior to that of angels. Many of the fathers and some moderns have thought that time is intended, and read it for a little while; but this is not true, for Christ continues in the nature which he assumed, though it be now refined and perfected. The inferiority of nature is admitted, but that inferiority is, as it were, compensated by a superiority of honour and glory. Then admit candidly how the Apostle handles his text. He looks to the thing itself as exhibited in the person of Christ, rather than to the exact meaning of the words, and presents to our meditation the glory after the resurrection, whereas the psalm extends the honour to all the gifts with which man is adorned by God's bounty; but in this embellishment, which leaves the literal sense entire, there is nothing unsuitable or improper. The sense comes to this, that Christ, having passed through death, was exalted into the glory which he has obtained. Guard it at once against a false inference. It is not that Christ obtained anything for himself individually, as those say who have devised the notion that he first earned eternal life for himself and afterwards for us; only the way or means of obtaining glory is indicated here. Note too the end for which he is crowned, that every knee should bow to him, and reason from that final cause that all things are delivered into his hand. Then take the reference to his death as guarding his dignity rather than diminishing it, for when we hear how much good has been obtained for us there is no place left for contempt, since admiration of the divine goodness fills the whole mind. On the tasting of death, say that it means more than that he might be an example to others, as one father held, comparing a physician who tastes a bitter draught first that the patient may not refuse it; it means that Christ died for us, and that by taking upon him what was due to us he redeemed us from the curse of death. On the refinement which makes tasting a mere touching of the lips, because Christ emerged from death a conqueror, neither refute nor condemn it, but doubt whether the Apostle meant to speak so finely; for to taste food, in the language of Scripture, is to eat it, and to taste death is to die. And add that all this was done through grace, since the cause of redemption was the infinite love of God towards us, through which he spared not even his own Son.

Say first what is now visible and to whom it belongs: this is done only with regard to Jesus, God and man, who is now crowned with glory and honour as a reward for having suffered death, and who was made a little lower than the angels, who can neither suffer nor die. Then take the whole weight of the verse into the last clause, and expound the tasting of death as fully as it will bear. Set out the case that made it necessary. In consequence of the fall of Adam the whole human race became sinful in nature, and in practice added transgression to sinfulness of disposition, and so became exposed to endless perdition; to redeem them, Jesus Christ took on him the nature of man and suffered the penalty due to their sins. Then explain the figure in the word, for it was a custom in ancient times to take off criminals by making them drink a cup of poison. Recall how Socrates was adjudged by the Athenian magistrates to drink the juice of hemlock, though the sentence was one of the most unjust ever pronounced on man, since he was not only innocent of every crime laid to his charge but was the greatest benefactor to his country; and how, when the officer brought in the poison and his friends urged that he still had time to live, he refused to avail himself of a few remaining moments, seized the cup, and drank it off with the utmost cheerfulness. Then turn the picture round, for the reference in the text seems to point out the whole human race as accused, tried, found guilty and condemned, each having his own poisoned cup to drink; and Jesus takes the cup out of the hand of each and cheerfully drinks off the dregs. Ask whether this is not the cup he spoke of when he prayed that it might pass from him, and answer that without his drinking it the salvation of the world would have been impossible, so that he drank it in the place of every human soul. State the four things the verse settles: that Jesus Christ was incarnated; that he suffered death as an expiatory victim; that the persons in whose behalf he suffered were the whole human race, every man, that ever was or will be born into the world; and that all this was by the grace, the mercy, the infinite goodness of God. Note last the rival reading, which some manuscripts and one ancient version give as without God, meaning that the manhood died and not the Deity; treat it as probably a marginal gloss which crept into the text, though it is quoted by some of the chief Greek and Latin fathers.

debates.question: Does a little lower mean a little in degree, or for a little while?

sides.position: In degree, since that is plainly the psalm's sense; and Christ still continues in the nature he assumed, though it is now refined and perfected, so the inferiority is compensated by a superiority of honour
In degree, of the rank assumed on earth; the rendering a little while is much less probable
Of time, for a little while, since as the eternal Word he could not die and a body was prepared for him

debates.question: How can it be said that he was crowned in order to taste death?

sides.position: The efficacy of the sufferings depends on their triumphant issue, and a Christian cannot separate the two even in thought
The crowning is the reward of the dying and not its purpose; the preposition is causal
Christ is crowned to this end, that every knee should bow, whence we may reason that all things are delivered into his hand

debates.question: What is the force of tasting death?

sides.position: A familiar Hebraism
Not a rapid sip but a bitter experience, the seeing of death
To taste food in Scripture is to eat it, and to taste death is to die; the refinement that makes it a touching of the lips is neither refuted nor accepted
The draining of the poisoned cup which each condemned man owed, taken out of every hand and drunk to the dregs

debates.question: By the grace of God, or apart from God?

sides.position: By the grace of God, the cause of redemption being his infinite love
The rival reading, meaning that the manhood died and not the Deity, is probably a marginal gloss that crept into the text, though quoted by chief Greek and Latin fathers

outliers.note: Alone expounds the tasting of death from the ancient custom of despatching criminals with a cup of poison, recalling the injustice of the sentence on Socrates and the cheerfulness with which he drank, and turning it into the picture of a condemned race whose cups are all drunk by another.

Alone notices what the verse conspicuously refrains from saying, that we see all things put in subjection unto Jesus, and observes that other words of the psalm are substituted precisely because the subjection is not yet complete.

themes: we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels
crowned with glory and honour
that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man

10.pericope_label: It became him to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings

schools.summary: Take the impersonal verb in its proper force, an old word meaning to stand out, to be becoming or seemly, and be careful whom the pronoun designates: it is in the dative and refers to God the Father, not to Christ, as the following mention of the author makes plain. The voluntary humiliation of the Son a little lower than the angels was a seemly thing to the Father, and the passage that follows is worthy to stand beside the great hymn of the second chapter of Philippians. On the two prepositions, mark the distinction: for whom expresses the reason or final cause of the universe, and through whom, with the genitive, the agent by whom the universe came into existence, which is a direct repudiation of the notion of intermediate agencies between God and creation. The universe comes out of God, by means of God, and for God. On the title given to Christ, trace the word through its other occurrences. In one place it bears its original meaning of Leader; in two others the idea of leading the way has passed into that of origination, so that Author is the best rendering. Yet in a context which so distinctly presents our Lord as taking on himself the conditions of man's lot, and so passing into the glory which he wins for man, the primary thought of leading must not be entirely set aside: he is a pioneer blazing the way, the leader of the sons of God, and the Elder Brother of us all. On the making perfect, remove the scruple at once. If anyone recoils at the idea of God making Christ perfect, let him bear in mind that it is the humanity of Jesus that is under discussion; nothing is said of sin, and the opposite is asserted elsewhere in this Epistle. It is by means of sufferings that God perfected his Son in his human nature, and there are three aspects of this in the Epistle: by his suffering unto death he bare the sins of many, he offered the sacrifice of a perfect obedience, and he was enabled to be a perfect representative of man. This last thought pervades the remaining verses of the chapter. On the eleventh verse, take the special meaning which sanctify carries in this Epistle, a bringing into fellowship with God, the Holy One, and note that those who are sanctified are literally those who are being sanctified, since it is a process and not a single completed act. Then read the phrase all of one as of one Father, which is the connecting link with the preceding verse and its many sons; and observe that even before the incarnation there was a kinship, though we are not sons in the full sense that he is. Because of the common Father he is not ashamed to own us as brethren, unworthy sons though we be.

State the object of the passage plainly: it is to make Christ's humiliation appear glorious to the godly. When he is said to have been clothed with our flesh he seems to be classed with the common order of men, and the cross brought him lower than all men; we must therefore take heed lest Christ should be less esteemed because he willingly humbled himself for us. The Apostle shows that this very thing ought to be deemed honourable to the Son of God, that by these means he was consecrated the Captain of our salvation. Then attend to the circumlocution used instead of the bare name of God. He might by one word have named him, but his purpose was to remind us that what is to be deemed best is that which he appoints, whose will and glory are the right end of all things; no better cause can be found than the good pleasure of God, for as all things are sustained by his power, so all things ought to serve his glory. Then show why this way was necessary, and find the reason in the ordinary way God deals with his own people. His will is to exercise them with various trials, so that they may spend their whole life under the cross; it was hence necessary that Christ, as the firstbegotten, should by the cross be inaugurated into his supremacy, since that is the common lot and condition of all. This is the conforming of the head with the members. Draw the consolation out of it and let it be felt as consolation: it is a singular thing, calculated to mitigate the bitterness of the cross, when the faithful hear that by sorrows and tribulations they are sanctified for glory as Christ himself was, and hence they see a sufficient reason why they should lovingly kiss the cross rather than dread it. On the eleventh verse, take it as proving that what was said had to be fulfilled in the person of Christ on account of his connection with his members, and as teaching that his putting on our flesh was a remarkable evidence of the divine goodness. On the disputed words all of one, note that they are commonly understood of one Adam and that some refer them to God, not without reasons; prefer that one nature is meant, as though he had said they are made out of the same mass, and let the fourteenth verse decide the question. Then say what follows for our confidence. It avails not a little that we are united to the Son of God by a bond so close that we can find in our own nature the holiness of which we are in want; for he not only as God sanctifies us, but there is also the power of sanctifying in his human nature, not that it has it from itself, but that God poured upon it a perfect fullness of holiness, so that from it we may all draw.

Say what the fitness was and to what it was suitable: it was suitable to all God's attributes, to his justice, his goodness and his wisdom, and it accorded with the Divine wisdom, the requisitions of justice and the economy of grace to offer Jesus as a sacrifice in order to bring many sons and daughters to glory. Take the two prepositions as marking the ultimate end and the first cause, God being both the cause of all things and the end of them. Then state the bare necessity, since it is the answer to the objection behind the verse: without suffering he could not have died, and without dying he could not have made an atonement for sin, so that the sacrifice had to be consummated in order that he might be qualified to be the Captain or Author of the salvation of men and to lead all who become children of God through faith into eternal glory. Note that this answers the grand objection of the Jews, that the Messiah is never to be conquered or to die but will be victorious and endure for ever; the Apostle shows that this is not the counsel of God, and that on the contrary it was entirely congruous to the will and nature of God to bring men to eternal glory through the suffering and death of the Messiah. Say that without the passion and death of Christ the salvation of man would have been impossible. On the word rendered perfect, take it as consummation, the bringing of him to a full and glorious end of all his troubles by his atoning sufferings for them. Then enter the caution that this passage most needs, and enter it firmly, for the words are easily abused. What is here said of our Lord's being made perfect through sufferings has no relation to our being saved or sanctified by sufferings. He himself was perfect, as God and as man, before ever he suffered; by his sufferings, in his life and death, he was made a perfect or complete sin-offering; but unless we were to be made the same sacrifice and to atone for sin, what is said of him in this respect is as much out of our sphere as his ascension into heaven. It is his atonement, and his Spirit carrying on the work of faith with power in our hearts, that alone can sanctify us. Allow what may truly be allowed and no more: various afflictions may indeed be made subservient to this, and so far as they are blessed to the weaning of us from sin, and to the causing of our affections to be set on things above, so far they do indirectly help on our sanctification. On the eleventh verse, take the word for sanctifying to mean making atonement or reconciliation, and read the last clause of one nature, since both the Sanctifier and the sanctified are of the same nature; and though as to his Godhead he is infinitely raised above men and angels, having become incarnate he blushes not to acknowledge all his true followers as his brethren.

Having mentioned the death of Christ, proceed now to prevent and remove the scandal of the cross, and do it two ways, by showing how it became God that Christ should suffer, and how much man is benefited by those sufferings. On the first, describe God as the final end and first cause of all things, and say that as such it became him to secure his own glory in all that he did, not only to act so that he might in nothing dishonour himself, but so that he might from everything have a revenue of glory. Then show that he acted up to this glorious character in the work of redemption, in the choice both of the end and of the means. In the choice of the end, which was to bring many sons to glory, both in the enjoyment of the glorious privileges of the gospel and in the future glory of heaven, which will be glory indeed, an exceeding and eternal weight of glory. Observe four things upon it. We must be the sons of God, both by adoption and by regeneration, before we can be brought to the glory of heaven, for heaven is the inheritance and only the children are heirs of it. All true believers are the children of God, since to those that receive Christ he has granted the power and privilege of being the children of God. Though the sons of God are but few in one place and at one time, yet when they shall all be brought together it will appear that they are many, for Christ is the firstborn among many brethren. And all the sons of God, however dispersed and divided now, shall at length be brought together to glory. Then take the choice of the means, and let the first of them be the finding out of such a person as should be the captain of our salvation; for those that are saved must come to that salvation under the guidance of a captain and leader sufficient for that purpose, and the passage tells us how he was made sufficient, namely by sufferings.

debates.question: To whom does it became him refer?

sides.position: To God the Father, as the following mention of the author makes plain, and not to Christ
To God as the final end and first cause of all things, whose glory had to be secured in the whole work

debates.question: What does the title captain mean?

sides.position: Author is the best rendering, since the idea of leading the way has passed into that of origination; but in this context the primary thought of leading must not be entirely set aside
Either sense suits: one leading off, a pioneer blazing the way, and also the Elder Brother of us all
Prince, leader and author of their salvation, by his atoning sufferings for them
A captain and leader sufficient for the purpose, under whose guidance the saved must come to salvation

debates.question: Does his being perfected through sufferings mean that we are sanctified by ours?

sides.position: No. He was perfect as God and as man before ever he suffered, and by suffering was made a complete sin-offering, which is as far out of our sphere as his ascension; afflictions help only indirectly, as they wean us from sin

Yes, in its own way: it was necessary that the firstbegotten should by the cross be inaugurated into his supremacy, since that is the common lot; and the faithful hear with consolation that by sorrows they are sanctified for glory as he was, and may kiss the cross rather than dread it
The scruple is misplaced, since it is the humanity that is under discussion and nothing is said of sin

debates.question: What does sanctify mean in the eleventh verse?

sides.position: To make atonement or reconciliation, answering to the Hebrew word for expiation, as in the saying that for their sakes I sanctify myself
Some would render the clause the expiator and the expiated; the word may bear it, but the fuller idea of consecration is richer and is to be preferred
Of the three senses the verb carries, purification from pollution is meant here, though others prefer expiation as suiting a passage about atonement
In this Epistle it means a bringing into fellowship with God, and the participle is a present, so that it is a process and not a completed act

debates.question: What is meant by all of one?

sides.position: One nature; father, family, blood, seed and race have all been proposed, but nature is confirmed by the close of the verse
Of one Father, which is the link with the many sons of the previous verse
Family, spirit, Father or nature: any of these will suit the connection

outliers.note: Alone enters a caution against a common misuse of the verse, insisting that what is said of the Lord's being perfected through sufferings has no relation to our being sanctified by ours, and that afflictions help only indirectly, as they wean us from sin.
Alone finds in the two prepositions a direct repudiation of intermediate agencies between God and the creation, since the universe comes out of God, by means of God, and for God.

themes: it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things
to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings
he is not ashamed to call them brethren

12.pericope_label: I will declare thy name unto my brethren; behold I and the children

schools.summary: Establish the character of the psalm first, since the argument rests on it. It is remarkable for its close connection with the narratives of the Passion; and whether the inscription which names David as author is correct, or whether, from the difficulty of finding any period in his history to which the expressions apply, we take the psalm to have been written after the Captivity, there can be no doubt of its Messianic character. Do not, however, class it with those psalms which are simply and directly prophetic, having no historic foreground, for the language of some of the verses is so definite and peculiar that we must regard it as descriptive of actual experience; call it rather typically prophetic of Christ. Then state exactly where the weight of the quotation falls, for this is easily mistaken. The point is not that he would declare God's name, but that he gave the name brethren to those whom he addressed. Explain why the argument is drawn from Scripture rather than from fact: it would have been easy to appeal to the plain record that the Redeemer used that word familiarly of his disciples, but since the readers had been Jews, and since it was necessary to show that what is maintained about the Messiah is found in the Old Testament, the appeal is made there. Note that both halves of the verse are in point: those to whom the Messiah declares God's name he calls brethren, and it is not alone but in a congregation of God's people that he sings the praise of God, which gives the picture of public worship with the Messiah sharing in it. On the thirteenth verse, take the two citations separately. The second is certainly from Isaiah; the first might be derived from the song of David or from another chapter of the same prophet, but since the words occur in the same chapter as the second we may with certainty consider that the source. Note the rare periphrastic form of the verb, and that the Messiah is represented as putting his trust in God as other men do. Then unfold what the second citation contributes. There the prophet, as the representative of God to the people, has uttered the divine message, and in these words retires into the same position with the people whom he has addressed, so that their relation towards God's word and the hope it inspires must be his also; and this twofold position of the prophet symbolised the twofold nature of him of whom every prophet was a type. Recall too that the prophet's sons were associated with him in his message, the warning of judgment and the promise being held up before the people inscribed in the symbolic names they bore. And mark that the children here are the same as the sons whom God was bringing to glory in the tenth verse, so that the chain of the argument holds.

Note first a small change in the citation: where the Greek version has one verb the Apostle uses another, the words being often used synonymously, only the latter includes the idea of a message, as it literally means to declare something from another. Then draw the doctrine out of the verse. It appears plainly that the proclamation of God's praises is always promoted by the teaching of the gospel, for as soon as God becomes known to us his boundless praises sound in our hearts and in our ears; and at the same time Christ encourages us by his own example publicly to celebrate them, so that they may be heard by as many as possible. Press why the celebration must be public: it would not be sufficient for each one of us to thank God privately for benefits received, unless we testify openly our gratitude and thus mutually stimulate one another. Then add what may serve as a most powerful stimulant and lead us most fervently to praise God, that Christ leads our songs and is the chief composer of our hymns. On the thirteenth verse, take the first clause as probably drawn from the psalm where the same words are found, though they occur also in the song of David and in the prophet. Defend that reference against the objection that the psalm has nothing of the Messiah in it. The whole psalm concerns one who was eminently a type of the Messiah, and in that sense the Messiah is no doubt found there; as God was to David his trust in all trials, so he was to the Son of David. Add the argument from its contents, which show clearly that David spoke in the person of another. There appeared in David but a faint shadow of the greatness which is there set forth in terms so magnificent: he boasts that he was made the head of the heathen, and that even aliens and people unknown willingly surrendered themselves to him at the report of his name; but David subdued a few neighbouring and well known nations by force of arms and made them tributaries, which was nothing to the extensive dominions of many other kings. Where was the voluntary submission? Where were the people so remote that he knew them not? Let the question stand, for it settles the reference. And note that another verse of the same psalm is applied elsewhere to Christ, respecting the calling of the Gentiles.

Take the declaring of the name as the substance of the gospel ministry: Christ declares the name of God, gracious and merciful, plenteous in goodness and truth, to all who believe, that they also may praise him. Show where and how this was done. The Apostle certainly quotes the psalm as referring to Jesus Christ, and these words as spoken by Christ to the Father in reference to his incarnation, as if he had said, when I shall be incarnated I will declare thy perfections to mankind, and among my disciples I will give glory to thee for thy mercy to the children of men. Point to the fulfilment: no man hath seen God at any time, but the Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him; nor were the perfections of God ever properly known or declared till the manifestation of Christ. Add another instance, when in that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit and thanked the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that he had hid these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them unto babes; thus he gave praise to God. Then take the second half of the verse and let it be sung rather than argued. In the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee: he is there as the precentor of the choir, and this he did literally, in the midst of his apostles, on the night before his passion; and as the words mean in a more general sense the setting forth of the praise of God, he has done it in the church by his word and his Spirit, he still does it, and will do it throughout all generations. On the thirteenth verse, take the two clauses as two acknowledgments of his nearness to us. As one that has communion with his brethren in sufferings as well as in nature he says, I will put my trust in him, to carry me through them all; and with a like acknowledgment of his near relation to them, as younger brethren who were yet but in their childhood, he presents all believers to God, saying, behold I and the children whom thou hast given me. Then make an observation about method which governs all three quotations, for it saves much needless difficulty. The Apostle does not intend to say that the portions quoted have any particular reference, taken by themselves, to the subject in question; they are only catch-words of whole paragraphs which, taken together, are full to the point, because they are prophecies of the Messiah and are fulfilled in him. This is evident from the last quotation, since the sentence goes on to say that the children are for signs and for wonders in Israel; and Jesus and his disciples wrought a multitude of the most stupendous signs and wonders in Israel, while the expression may also include all genuine Christians, who are for signs and wonders throughout the earth.

debates.question: Where is I will put my trust in him taken from?

sides.position: From the same chapter of Isaiah that certainly supplies the words which follow; the Greek matches the version exactly, the next verse is quoted immediately, and no other passage carries the expression
From a psalm of David, several parts of which seem to belong to the Messiah, since the psalm describes one who was eminently his type and its magnificence far outruns anything David achieved

debates.question: How do the quoted fragments carry the argument?

sides.position: They are only catch-words of whole paragraphs which, taken together, are full to the point, as appears from the last, where the children are for signs and wonders in Israel
Each division of the verse is separately in point, the one supplying the word brethren and the other the congregation in which he sings

outliers.note: Alone defends the Messianic reference of the disputed psalm by measuring its language against David's actual history, since the psalm boasts of unknown peoples yielding at the report of a name, whereas David subdued a few neighbouring nations by force of arms.

Alone states the principle governing all three citations, that the fragments do not bear the argument by themselves but are catch-words of whole paragraphs which, taken together, are full to the point.

themes: I will declare thy name unto my brethren
I will put my trust in him
Behold I and the children which God hath given me

14.pericope_label: He took part of the same, that he might destroy him that had the power of death

schools.summary: Note the order of the Greek, which has blood and flesh, the familiar order being departed from here as in one other place, and observe that this designation of human nature on its material side occurs four times in the New Testament and is extremely common in Jewish writers. Mark also that the two verbs differ: the children have become partners in blood and flesh, while of the same things he took part, and the emphasis of that statement is noteworthy, since his assumption of our nature had suffering and death for its object. On the verb rendered destroy, do not let it suggest killing. It is an old word meaning to render idle or ineffective, and is better given as bring to nought or annul his power; by means of his own death, paradoxical as it seems, Christ broke the power of the devil over death, certainly in men's fear of death. Explain in what sense that power was held: it was as the lord of sin, which is the cause and the sting of death, that the devil held dominion over death, or, as the words might mean, wielded the power possessed by death. Say plainly that death is the devil's realm because he is the author of sin, and that death as death is no part of the divine order; by meeting death himself the Redeemer vanquishes and destroys death for those he redeems. On the fifteenth verse, notice how the former misery and the present freedom are set side by side, and suppose the words prompted by the writer's intense sympathy with the persecuted and tempted readers whom he addresses; he writes throughout as one who never forgets their need of sympathetic help and who knows the power of the allurements and threats used to lead them into apostasy. The crushing power of the fear of death over those who have not grasped that in Christ life and immortality are brought to light is perhaps beyond any thought of ours to reach; the ancients feared death greatly, though their philosophers argued against it, and the phrase gives a graphic picture of bond-slaves of fear. On the sixteenth verse, prefer the marginal rendering, since the text as it stands introduces confusion into the argument: it is not of angels that he takes hold, but of the seed of Abraham. Allow that the verb probably cannot directly signify to help, as is often maintained, but insist that it distinctly suggests laying hold for the sake of giving help, and illustrate it from the Gospel narratives of our Lord's works of healing. Trace the language to the Old Testament, where God takes his people by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, and, in a still closer parallel, lays hold of the seed of Abraham from the ends of the earth; if those verses were in the writer's thought there is little need to ask why he chose that phrase rather than one of wider meaning.

Take the verse as an inference from what precedes and at the same time a fuller reason than has yet been given why it behoved the Son of God to put on our flesh, namely that he might partake of the same nature with us, and that by undergoing death he might redeem us from it. Say that the passage deserves especial notice, for it not only confirms the reality of the human nature of Christ but also shows the benefit which thence flows to us. Here his infinite love towards us appears; but its overflowing appears in this, that he put on our nature that he might thus make himself capable of dying, for as God he could not undergo death. Then examine the words about the destruction of the devil, since brevity here has been mistaken for vagueness. It imports this, that he cannot prevail against us; for though the devil still lives and constantly attempts our ruin, all his power to hurt us is destroyed or restrained. It is a great consolation to know that we have to do with an enemy who cannot prevail against us. On the fifteenth verse, say how miserable is the life of those who fear death, for they must feel it to be dreadful because they look on it apart from Christ, and then nothing but a curse appears in it; and whence is death but from God's wrath against sin? Hence is that bondage throughout life, a perpetual anxiety by which unhappy souls are tormented, for through a consciousness of sin the judgment of God is ever present to the view. From this fear Christ has delivered us, who by undergoing our curse has taken away what is dreadful in death; and though we are not now freed from death, yet in life and in death we have peace and safety when Christ goes before us. Then apply the test to the reader, and do not soften it: if anyone cannot pacify his mind by disregarding death, let him know that he has as yet made but very little proficiency in the faith of Christ, for as extreme fear is owing to ignorance of the grace of Christ, so it is a certain evidence of unbelief. On the sixteenth verse, note that the comparison enhances the benefit and the honour with which Christ has favoured us in putting on our flesh, for he never did so much for angels. As there had to be a remarkable remedy for man's dreadful ruin, it was the design of the Son of God that there should be some incomparable pledge of his love which angels had not in common with us; and that he preferred us to angels was owing not to our excellency but to our misery. There is therefore no reason for us to glory as though we were superior to angels, except that our heavenly Father has shown us the ampler mercy which we needed. Add that this one passage is abundantly sufficient to lay prostrate those who denied Christ to have been a real man, for it is not said that he became an angel clothed with angelic nature, but that he took upon him man's nature and not that of angels.

Say first who the children are, and take them widely: not only the disciples and all genuine Christians, but the whole human race, all Jews and all Gentiles. Support it from the saying that Jesus should die for that nation, and not for that nation only, but that he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad; and more plainly from the words that he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world. Explain why the language of the passage seems narrower than the doctrine: the Apostle is writing to Hebrews, and therefore uses in general a Jewish phraseology, pointing out to them their own privileges, and rarely introducing what the Messiah has done for the other nations of the earth. Then state the design of the incarnation from the verse: since those children of God who have fallen and are to be redeemed are human beings, in order to be qualified to redeem them by suffering and dying in their stead he himself likewise took part of the same, and thus he who was God with God became man with men. On the destroying, take it as a counterworking: by the merit of his own death, making atonement for sin, he renders useless and ineffectual all the operations of him who had the power to bring death into the world; so that death, which was intended by him who was a murderer from the beginning to be the final ruin of mankind, becomes the instrument of their exaltation and endless glory, and the death brought in by Satan is rendered ineffectual by the death of Christ. Note that death is the devil's servant and serjeant, delivering to him those whom he seizes in sin, and that the power was manifest to all though they saw not who exerted it. On the fifteenth verse, think first of those who had no revelation and no certainty of immortality, and were therefore continually in bondage to the fear of death, preferring life in any state to death because they had no hope beyond the grave. But say that all men naturally fear death, and that even those who have the fullest persuasion of a future state dread it, though genuine Christians, who know that if the earthly house of their tabernacle were dissolved they have a building of God eternal in the heavens, fear it not; for in the assurance they have of God's love the fear of death is removed, and by the purification of their hearts through faith the sting of death is extracted. Say that they who know not God are in continual torment through the fear of death, and that they fear death because they fear something beyond death, being conscious that they are wicked and terrified at the thought of eternity. On the sixteenth verse, prefer the marginal reading and give the word its full range, for it signifies not only to take hold of but to help, to succour, to save from sinking. The rebel angels sinned and were permitted to fall down until they fell into perdition; man sinned and was falling too, but Jesus laid hold on him and prevented him from falling into the bottomless pit.

Assert the incarnation from the sixteenth verse and let the negative carry as much weight as the positive: verily he took not upon him the nature of angels, but he took upon him the seed of Abraham. Though as God he pre-existed from all eternity, yet in the fullness of time he took our nature into union with his divine nature and became really and truly man; he did not lay hold of angels, but he laid hold of the seed of Abraham. Then say what became of those he passed by, and say it soberly. The angels fell, and he let them go, and lie under the desert, the defilement and the dominion of their sin, without hope or help. Christ never designed to be the Saviour of the fallen angels; as their tree fell, so it lies, and must lie to eternity, and therefore he did not assume their nature. Add the reason from the nature of the case, that the nature of angels could not be an atoning sacrifice for the sin of man. Then show what he did instead, and why. Resolving to recover the seed of Abraham and to raise them from their fallen state, he took upon him the human nature from one descended from the loins of Abraham, that the same nature which had sinned might suffer, so as to restore human nature to a state of hope and trial, and to bring all who accept of mercy to a state of special favour and salvation. Draw the encouragement out of it: now there is hope and help for the chief of sinners in and through Christ, for here is a price paid sufficient for all and suitable to all, since it was paid in our own nature. Close with the application the passage presses, and press it as a distinguishing mercy: let us all know the day of our gracious visitation, and improve that mercy which has been shown to fallen men and not to the fallen angels.

Warn the hearer at the outset not to pass lightly over what is said here, and do not let him think it a slight matter that the Son took on him our flesh. The Apostle, wishing to show the great kindness of God towards man and the love which he had for the human race, having said that since the children were partakers of blood and flesh he also himself likewise took part of the same, now follows up the subject; and the point of it is that he granted not this to angels, for verily he taketh not hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham. Ask what is meant by that, and answer plainly: he took not on him an angel's nature, but man's; he did not grasp that nature which belongs to angels, but ours. Then ask the finer question, why the word used is not simply he took upon him, but he taketh hold of; for the whole tenderness of the passage lies in that choice. The expression is derived from the figure of persons pursuing those who turn away from them, and doing everything to overtake them as they flee, and to take hold of them as they are bounding away. Apply the figure exactly. When human nature was fleeing from him, and fleeing far away, he pursued after us and overtook us; and he showed that he has done this only out of kindness, and love, and tender care. Set the comparison beside the earlier one in the Epistle for the same purpose. When it was asked whether the angels are not all ministering spirits sent forth to minister for those who shall be heirs of salvation, the writer was showing his extreme interest on behalf of human nature and how great account God makes of it; and in this place he sets it forth much more strongly by the same kind of comparison, saying that he taketh not hold of angels.

debates.question: Who are the children?

sides.position: All the children of God given to Christ, not the men of this world, nor Abraham's natural seed, nor visible professors, nor the apostles only
The whole human race, Jew and Gentile alike; the narrower language is Jewish phraseology natural in a letter to Hebrews

debates.question: What does destroy mean here?

sides.position: Bring to nought, annul his power; it was as lord of sin, the cause and the sting of death, that the devil held dominion over death
To render idle or ineffective; by means of his own death Christ broke the power of the devil over death, certainly in men's fear of it
Not to close life or to kill, but to bring into subjection and crush his dominion
That he cannot prevail against us: though the devil still lives and attempts our ruin, all his power to hurt us is destroyed or restrained
Counterworked, so that the death Satan brought in becomes the instrument of man's exaltation and endless glory

debates.question: Whose is the fear of death that held men in bondage?

sides.position: Chiefly the Gentiles, who had no revelation and no certainty of immortality; yet all men naturally fear death, and those who know not God fear what lies beyond it
The persecuted and tempted readers of the letter, whose need of sympathetic help the writer never forgets
Every man who knows not Christ, for every man who fears death is in a slavish and uncomfortable state
The believer as well: a man who cannot pacify his mind about death has made very little proficiency in faith, extreme fear being a certain evidence of unbelief
Not the Christian, who has nothing to fear on the dying bed, in the grave, or at the judgment, being everywhere under his Saviour's eye

debates.question: What is the force of he took not on him the nature of angels?

sides.position: The margin is right and the text confuses the argument: it is not of angels that he takes hold, but of the seed of Abraham; the verb suggests laying hold in order to help
The word is drawn from pursuing those who turn away, overtaking them as they flee and catching them as they bound off
Not a denial of help to the good angels, who do receive help from him, but a non-assumption of their nature, which could not die and so could not atone
The angels fell and he let them go; as their tree fell, so it lies, and their nature could not be an atoning sacrifice for the sin of man

outliers.note: Alone supplies the figure behind the verb, that it is drawn from pursuing those who turn away and doing everything to overtake them as they flee, so that when human nature was fleeing far away he pursued after and overtook us.

Alone supports the bondage to the fear of death with a long quotation from Hamlet on the dread of what dreams may come, and observes that this very dread restrains many miserable creatures from hurrying themselves into the unknown world.

themes: he also himself likewise took part of the same
that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death
he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham

17.pericope_label: A merciful and faithful high priest, able to succour them that are tempted

schools.summary: Take the opening adverb as one of cause, a use frequent in this Epistle, and give the verb its proper force: it is the old word for owing, whether money, or service and love, or duty. Having undertaken the work of redemption voluntarily, Jesus was thereafter under obligation to be properly equipped for that priestly service and sacrifice. Join the phrase in all things to the being made like, and set out what the likeness must include: like his brethren he must be liable to, and must suffer, temptation, sorrow, pain and death. Name the one exception plainly, the yielding to sin, and admit how difficult it may be for us to comprehend real temptation in the Son of God who is also the Son of man; yet he knew what temptation was, and fought through to victory. Render the next clause that he might prove, or become, a compassionate and faithful High Priest, and explain why the likeness was indispensable: the high priest was the representative of men to God, and without such likeness he could be no true High Priest for man. Note that the order of the Greek throws an emphasis on compassionate, which is in full harmony with the pervading tone of the chapter, and state the principle behind that emphasis: one who has not so understood the infirmities of his brethren as to be compassionate cannot be their faithful representative before God. Attach the word faithful more closely to what follows, for if it is through the power of sympathy gained by sufferings that he becomes compassionate, it is through the suffering of death that he proves himself the faithful High Priest in things pertaining to God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. Observe that the two adjectives touch the chief points in the function of a high priest, sympathy with men and fidelity toward God, and sharpen the contrast by recalling that the high priests of that generation were political and ecclesiastical tools, chosen by Rome and out of sympathy with the people. Note also that the title, hereafter so prominent, is brought in somewhat suddenly, though several expressions in the chapter have prepared for it; and that the characteristic function of the high priest was his presentation of the sacrifice on the Day of Atonement. On the last verse, take the word tempted in its wider Greek sense, to put to the proof, whether by afflictions which try a man's character or by an inducement to evil, and say that the Saviour was subjected to both in as severe a form as was ever presented to men. Make the perfect tense permanent, a lasting part of his experience, and trace the temptation to escape the shame of the cross from the wilderness, through the rebuke to Peter, to Gethsemane. Let the word able strike the heart of it: his power to help is due not merely to his deity as God's Son but also to his humanity, without which he could not sympathise; and the verb rendered succour is a compound meaning to run at a cry for help. Say last for whom it was written, that these readers were daily tempted to give up Christ and to apostatise, and that he understands their predicament and is able to help them to be faithful.

Distinguish two things in Christ's human nature before expounding the verse, the real flesh and the affections or feelings which belong to a man; and teach that he had not only put on the real flesh but also all those feelings. Then show the benefit which hence proceeds, for this is the true teaching of faith, that we find in our own case the reason why the Son of God undertook our infirmities. Say why the doctrine must be held so, and not held coldly: all knowledge without a felt need of this benefit is cold and lifeless. Then notice how the sentence is constructed, for there is here an arrangement such as is often found in the prophets. Set the members out in lines and the correspondence appears: that compassionate he might be; and a faithful high priest in the things of God; to make an atonement for the sins of the people; for as he suffered, being himself tempted, he can help the tempted. The first line and the last correspond, and the second and the third.
