He is compassionate because he can sympathise with the tempted, having been himself tempted; and he is a true and faithful high priest because he really expiated the sins of the people; and that he might be all this, he became like his brethren by taking their nature. Then say why mercy is especially required in this office, for the reasoning turns on it. In a priest, whose office it is to appease God's wrath, to help the miserable, to raise up the fallen and to relieve the oppressed, mercy is especially required, and it is what experience produces in us, since it is a rare thing for those who are always happy to sympathise with the sorrows of others. Note that a saying of the poet, that one not ignorant of evil learns to succour the wretched, was no doubt derived from daily examples found among men. Then guard the application at once, since it must not be pressed into an argument about what the Son of God lacked. He had no need of experience that he might know the emotions of mercy; but we could not have been persuaded that he is merciful and ready to help us, had he not become acquainted by experience with our miseries. On the last verse, say simply that having been tried by our evils he is ready to bring us help; that the word rendered temptation here means no other thing than experience or probation; and that to be able, in this place, is to be fit, or inclined, or suitable to that office of helping.

Say why the likeness was necessary and to what end: because he thus laid hold on man in order to redeem him, it was necessary that he should in all things become like to man, that he might suffer in his stead and make an atonement in his nature. Take in all things to mean all that essentially pertains to human nature, and all sufferings and temptations. Then divide the two titles between their objects, merciful toward sinners and faithful toward God, and define the office: a priest or high priest is one who has a right of approaching God and of bringing others to him. On the mercy, say that he might be affected with a feeling of our infirmities, so that, partaking of our nature with all its innocent infirmities and afflictions, he might know how to compassionate poor, afflicted, suffering man. On the fidelity, say that it is exercised in those things which relate to God, whose justice requires the punishment of transgressors or a suitable expiation for the sins of the people; and note that the proper meaning of the phrase is to make propitiation or atonement for sins by sacrifice. Then set out the two sides of this priesthood. He exercises himself in the things pertaining to God, taking heed that God's honour be properly secured, his worship properly regulated, his laws properly enforced, and both his justice and his mercy magnified. And he exercises himself in things pertaining to men, that he may make an atonement for them, apply that atonement to them, and liberate them from the curse of a broken law, from the guilt and power of sin, and from all the evils to which they were exposed by it, and at last open their way into the holiest by his own blood. On the final verse, state the maxim on which it is founded: a state of suffering disposes persons to be compassionate, and those who endure most afflictions are they who feel most for others. Support it, if you will, from the poet who wrote that having himself been distressed he learns to pity woes so like his own. Then name what tempted believers stand in need of, which is threefold: strength to withstand their temptations, consolation to support their spirits under them, and seasonable deliverance from them; and show how the succour of this High Priest is suited to each and variously administered, by his word and promises, by his Spirit communicating supplies of grace and strong consolation and rebuking their tempters, and by his providence disposing all things to their good in the issue. Close by giving the tempted their particular claim: those who are peculiarly tempted and severely tried have an especial interest in Christ, and may go with boldness to the throne of grace, where they shall assuredly obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need. Were the rest of Scripture silent on this subject, this verse might be an ample support for every tempted soul.

debates.question: How is the seventeenth verse constructed?

sides.position: As the prophets often build: compassionate, then faithful high priest, then the atonement, then the helping of the tempted, so that the first member answers the last and the second the third
The Greek order throws an emphasis on compassionate, while faithful is more closely connected with the words that follow, so that the fidelity is proved by the suffering of death
The two adjectives touch the chief points in the office, sympathy with men and fidelity toward God

debates.question: What does it behoved him express?

sides.position: Obligation incurred by a voluntary undertaking: having undertaken redemption freely, he was bound to be properly equipped for that priestly service
Fitness and propriety, that nothing should be wanting in respect of the innocent propensities and sympathies of human nature
Necessity, in order to his design of redeeming them

debates.question: How does his own suffering make him able to succour?

sides.position: By the maxim that a state of suffering disposes men to be compassionate, and those who endure most feel most for others
His power to help rests not merely on his deity but on his humanity, without which he could not sympathise
He needed no experience in order to know the emotions of mercy, but we could not have been persuaded that he is ready to help us had he not become acquainted by experience with our miseries
One who has never been sick, or buried a friend, or been tempted, is poorly qualified to impart consolation in such scenes

outliers.note: Alone sharpens the two adjectives by contrast with the high priests of that generation, who were political and ecclesiastical tools and puppets, chosen by Rome and out of sympathy with the people.

Alone sets out a threefold analysis of what tempted believers need — strength to withstand, consolation to support, and seasonable deliverance — with the ways in which the succour is administered, by the word, by the Spirit, and by providence.

themes: in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren
a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God
he is able to succour them that are tempted
